extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in freedom of expression, individuality, and the limits of social control
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical guidance about when opinions and actions should be permitted or restricted, and about the moral conduct of public discussion and individuality. Covers grounds for free expression, limits where speech incites harm, and the social value of individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion may be true (do not silence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not suppress opinions merely because they are unpopular; silencing risks eliminating true beliefs. This is offered as the first of four distinct grounds for freedom of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous opinions may contain part of the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the silenced opinion be an error, it may, and very commonly does, contain a portion of truth; and since the general or prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely or never the whole truth, it is only by the collision of adverse opinions that the remainder of the truth has any chance of being supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit open collision of ideas because even false doctrines can contribute elements of truth; suppression prevents correction and completion of prevailing views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Received opinion must be contestable to avoid prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the received opinion be not only true, but the whole truth; unless it is suffered to be, and actually is, vigorously and earnestly contested, it will, by most of those who receive it, be held in the manner of a prejudice, with little comprehension or feeling of its rational grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage vigorous contestation of orthodoxies so adherents understand rational bases; preventing contest leads to dogmatic, uncomprehending belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contestation preserves the meaning and vitality of doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of the doctrine itself will be in danger of being lost, or enfeebled, and deprived of its vital effect on the character and conduct: the dogma becoming a mere formal profession, inefficacious for good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular dispute keeps doctrines lively and effective; without it dogma becomes hollow and unpersuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech may be restricted when it positively instigates harmful acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions lose their immunity when the circumstances in which they are expressed are such as to constitute their expression a positive instigation to some mischievous act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressions that create a direct, causal incitement (e.g., addressing an excited mob in front of a target) may justly be punished; mere circulation in press is different from oral provocation of immediate violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle for actions: do not make yourself a nuisance
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts, of whatever kind, which, without justifiable cause, do harm to others, may be, and in the more important cases absolutely require to be, controlled... The liberty of the individual must be thus far limited; he must not make himself a nuisance to other people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals should be free to act on their opinions provided their actions do not unjustifiably harm others; social control is warranted when actions cause harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law should not police intemperate or sophistical argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal offences of the kind are... to argue sophistically, to suppress facts or arguments, to misstate the elements of the case, or misrepresent the opposite opinion... still less could law presume to interfere with this kind of controversial misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresentation and sophistry in debate are morally blameworthy but difficult to legislate against; social and critical opinion, not legal sanction, should address them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid calumny and stigmatizing opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst offence of this kind which can be committed by a polemic, is to stigmatize those who hold the contrary opinion as bad and immoral men. To calumny of this sort, those who hold any unpopular opinion are peculiarly exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public discussion should condemn personal attacks and moral stigmatization of dissenters because they especially silence and injure minorities; reserve criticism for arguments, not persons' morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minority views require studied moderation of language to obtain a hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions contrary to those commonly received can only obtain a hearing by studied moderation of language, and the most cautious avoidance of unnecessary offence...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those advancing unpopular views should use measured language and avoid unnecessary offence to be heard; by contrast, prevailing opinions may more easily use vituperation to deter dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn advocacy marked by want of candour, malignity, or intolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion ought... to condemn every one, on whichever side of the argument he places himself, in whose mode of advocacy either want of candour, or malignity, bigotry, or intolerance of feeling manifest themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion should judge advocates by fairness and honesty of their representation of opponents' positions; praise should go to those who state opposing views calmly and honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to act on opinions (experiments of living)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us next examine whether the same reasons do not require that men should be free to act upon their opinions — to carry these out in their lives, without hindrance, either physical or moral, from their fellow-men, so long as it is at their own risk and peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should allow individuals to 'experiment' with modes of living and carry opinions into practice, provided no unjustifiable harm to others ensues; variety of experiments serves social knowledge and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of individuality: freedom and variety of situations
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of man... is the highest and most harmonious development of his powers to a complete and consistent whole; that, for this there are two requisites, 'freedom, and variety of situations;' and that from the union of these arise 'individual vigour and manifold diversity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and social institutions should preserve freedom and diverse circumstances to cultivate individuality, originality, and human development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice exercises and strengthens faculties; blind conformity weakens them
rubrics_metrics.description: The human faculties of perception, judgment, discriminative feeling, mental activity, and even moral preference, are exercised only in making a choice... He who does anything because it is the custom, makes no choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage autonomous choice rather than mere conformity because active choice develops reasoning, judgment, and moral character; overreliance on custom produces inert, 'machine-like' individuals.
